This Rule was issued on an application under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure for quashing the proceeding of Uttara Poshchim Police Station Case No. 16(12)19 dated 9-12-2019 corresponding to GR Case No. 555 of 2019 under sections 406/420/506 of the Penal Code, 1860 now pending in the Court of learned Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka. 

 5. Learned Advocates Ms. Sufia Ahmed along with Mr. Imtiaz Moinul Islam by filing supplementary affidavit appearing on behalf of the accused-petitioner at the very outset she submits that fact of the FIR is true. There were monetary transactions in between the parties. The petitioner consumed the loan money. Then for scarcity of money some amount was paid and some was remained unpaid. For realization of outstanding dues he filed this case under sections 406/420/506 of the Penal Code. She further submits that the transactions were in between the two businessmen. They have transacted money with each other with mutual understanding and there was no initial deception which is the ingredient of section 420 of the Penal Code. There was an agreement MOU in between them and subsequently the complainant helped the accused-petitioner for obtaining bail. Pointing this relationship learned Advocate submits that there was good and friendly relationship with each other. There was no any iota of statement made in the complaint petition which suggest to constitute offence under sections406/420 of the Penal Code. In support of her submission learned Advocate for the petitioner cited good number of decisions, the cases of Mujib-ud-Doula Bhuiyan (Md) vs State and another, reported in 71 DLR 634, Dewan Obaidur Rahman vs State and another, 4 BLC (AD)167, Abdur Rouf (Md) alias Nayan vs State and another, 53 DLR 283, Syed Ali Mir and another vs Syed Omor Ali and another, 10 BID (AD) 168 : 42 DLR (AD) 240, Md Islam Ali Mia alias Md Islam vs Atnal Chandra Mondal and another, 13 BLD (AD) 28 : 45 DLR (AD) 27, Islam Ali Mia alias Md Islam vs Amal Chandra Mondal and another, 45 DLR (AD) 27 and the case of Jahanara Begum vs The State, 1985 BCR (AD) 281. 

 6. On the other hand learned Advocate Mr. Murad Reza (former Additional Attorney-General) along with learned Advocate Mr. Redwan Ahmed appearing on behalf of the opposite party No. 2 filed affidavit-in-opposition. Bone content of his submission is that there is no criminal proceeding pending against accused-petitioner. The case is under investigation. No cognizance yet to be taken by the competent Court. For invoking section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure there must be criminal proceeding and since there is no proceeding because it is the case under investigation. Whether charge-sheet or final report will be submitted it is unknown. He further submits that before taking cognizance and absence of criminal proceeding section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure cannot be invoked or cannot file before this Court. In support of his submission he also cited good number of decisions, the cases of Abdul Huque and others vs State, reported in 60 DLR (AD) Page 1, Anti Corruption Commission vs AAM Habibur Rahman and another, 67 DLR (AD) 278, Nasiruddin Mahmud & others vs Momtazuddin, 36 DLR (AD)14, Arifur Rahmanalias Bablu vs Shantosh Kumar Sadhu and another, 46 DLR (AD) 180, Md Shafiaul Anowar vs The State and another, 11 ADC 863, Haji Alauddin vs The State and another, 6 ADC 165 and Khondaker Mahtabuddin Ahmed and others vs State 49 DLR (AD) 132. 

 10. Learned Advocate for the opposite party No. 2 submitted that cognizance was not taken yet. But it is noted herein above that after initiation of the criminal proceeding there are no nexus in between taking cognizance or not. Taking cognizance is a matter of course of Court proceeding, if the content of the FIR or complaint does not disclose offence it must be buried as early as possible. Now the question approached to me what we mean by word proceeding, more particularly in this case criminal proceeding it needs to be discussed with authoritative meaning of word criminal proceeding. Learned Advocate for the opposite party very strongly submitted that there was no proceeding against the accused-petitioner. Therefore, section 561A of the CrPC does not attract in the instant case.  30. Mr. Murad Reza, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party No. 2, contested the Rule and has brought to our notice that the case is still under investigation and charge-sheet has not been submitted. Thus, no cognizance has yet been taken and the case is still pending before the Court of Chief Metropolitan Magistrate. He submits that before taking cognizance of a case by a competent Court or Tribunal proceedings cannot be said to be pending and therefore, the same cannot be quashed unless cognizance in respect thereof has been taken and process issued. Hence, the present application under section 561A of the Code is premature and not tenable in the eye of law. In support of his submission, he relied upon the decision of the case of Abdul Huque vs The State, reported in 60 DLR (AD) 1. 

 31. Relying on the decision of N. Mahmud vs M. Ahmed, reported in 36 DLR (AD) 14, he submits that the statutory power of Police to investigate cognizable offence cannot be interfere with under section 561A of the Code. Initial Stage does not mean any stage before submission of the charge-sheet by the police, but it means a stage after submission of the charge-sheet. According to the learned Advocate, proceeding before a Court starts only when the Magistrate takes cognizance of an offence on the basis of a police report or complaint. Before such cognizance is taken, there is no proceeding that can be quashed under section 561A of the Code. 

 32. Relying on the decision of ACC vs AAM Habibur Rahman, reported in 67 DLR (AD) 278, Mr. Reza submits that the document submitted by the defendants cannot be entertained at the initial stage. In the aforesaid decision, it was observed by our Apex Court that the documents and papers submitted by the Accused-Petitioner are to be examined by the Investigation Officer during the investigation stage at this initial stage of the investigation, there is no scope to consider the defense documents. He further submits that the allegations against the accused-petitioner cannot be determined without examination of the witnesses and evidence as decided in Haji Alauddin vs the State and another, reported in 6 ADC 165. 

 36. In the instant case, the petitioner has challenged the proceeding of Uttara Poshchim Police Station Case No. 16(12)19 dated 9-12-2019, corresponding to GR Case No. 555 of 2019 under sections 406, 420, and 506 of the Penal Code-1860. 

 38. On the other hand, the learned Advocate appearing for opposite party No. 2 submits that in the instant case, cognizance has not yet been taken by the competent Court of jurisdiction, and the matter is under investigation. As such, the Rule issued under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure is premature. In support of his submission, he relied upon the decision given in the case of Abdul Haque vs State, reported in 60 DLR (AD) 1.

Ms. Sufia Ahmed, learned Advocate for the petitioner cited good number of decisions, I have gone through the decisions, namely Syed Ali Mir and another vs Syed Omer Ali and another, reported in 10 BLD (AD) 168 : 42 DLR (AD) 240, Islam Ali Mia vs Amal Chandra Mondal and another, reported in 45 DLR (AD) 27, Jahanara Begum vs the State, BCR 1985 (AD) 281, Syeed Ahmed (Major) vs The State reported, in 32 DLR 247. In all the decisions referred to above, the proceeding was challenged after taking cognizance of the case. Thus the decisions as referred by the learned Advocate for the petitioner will not anyway, help the petitioner.

The Chief Justice of the West Pakistan High Court quashed the proceedings of the cases although the cases were at the complaint stage. While granting leave to appeal, the Supreme Court of Pakistan observed,

In Abdul Quader Chowdhury and others vs The State, 28 DLR (AD) 38, the Anti-Corruption Branch submitted charge-sheet under sections 417 and 109 of the Penal Code read with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 against the accused persons. After receipt of the charge-sheet and being satisfied about the prima facie case, the Magistrate issued warrant of arrest. Both the High Court Division and the Appellate Division refused to quash the proceedings. In this case, the apex Court considered the question as to when and under what circumstances the inherent jurisdiction under section 561A can and should be exercised. It was observed, 

 80. In Bangladesh vs Tan Kheng Hock, 31 DLR (AD) 69, charge-sheet was submitted under sections 156(8) and 156(89) of the Customs Act read with section 25B of the Special Powers Act. At the time of hearing the Rule the State filed counter affidavits in the High Court Division bringing on record the contents of the charge-sheet. The High Court Division quashed the proceedings soon after submission of the charge-sheet but before taking cognizance of the offence by the Court competent to try the case, The Appellate Division considered facts of the case and a good member of decisions including Emperor is Khwaja Nazir Ahmed, Raja Huq Nawaz and Abdul Quader Chowdhury in reaching the decision. While allowing the appeal, it was held, 

 82. In Narsiruddin Mahmud and others vs Mamtazuddin Ahmed and another, 36 DLR (AD) H, the complaint petition was filed under sections 420 and 406 of the Penal Code. The Sub-Divisional Magistrate sent the complaint to the concerned police station for treating it as FIR and for investigation. The accused persons obtained bail and moved the High Court Division for quashing the proceeding while the case was under investigation. The Rule was discharged. By a majority decision, the Appellate Division allowed the appeal and quashed the proceeding on merit. Abdul Quader Chowdhury was referred to on point of quashing the proceeding at "initial stage". In a separate judgment Chowdhury ATM Masud, J agreed that the complaint did not disclose any offence but expressed the view that proceeding before a Court starts when the Magistrate takes cognizance of an offence, on police report or on complaint and that before such cognizance, there is no proceeding that may be quashed under section 561A- Nevertheless, His Lordship observed that as the complaint-petition does not disclose a prime facie criminal case and as no proceeding is pending in any Court the appropriate, order should be that the complaint be treated as dismissed, and, the appellant should be, discharged from the, bail bond Shahabuddin Ahmed, J. (as he was then), in a separate judgment, found merit in the case and held that the FIR did not prima facie disclose commission of any criminal offence, but he was of the view that "initial stage" as referred to in Abdul Quader Chowdhury does not mean any stage prior to submission of the charge-sheet, but it means a stage after submission of the charge-sheet and accordingly, there is no legal basis for making an order quashing the proceeding at that stage simply on the ground that there was no proceeding against the accused in the eye of law. In the facts and circumstances of the case, Shahabuddin Ahmed, J concluded that the appropriate course would be to direct the police to complete the investigation and submit report within a short time, say 3(three) months and to keep the appeal pending and thus, interference with the investigation by the police can be avoided. 

 83. In Syed Mohammad Hashem alias Hashim vs State 48 DLR (AD) 87, charge-sheet was submitted under sections 467, 468, 420, 471 and 109 of the Penal Code. The Magistrate took cognizance of the offence and issued process. The Appellate Division was of the view that the FIR and the charge-sheet disclosed prima facie commission of offence. The petition was dismissed. On the issue as to what stage of the proceeding, the High Court Division can interfere under section 561A  of the Code, it was observed, 

 "It may be mentioned that the Privy Council in the case of Emperor vs Nazir Ahmad AIR (32) 1945 PC 18 approved the view taken in a Madras case that the High Court Division may interfere under section 561A  even during Police investigation if no cognizable offence is disclosed and still more if no offence of any kind is disclosed because in that case the Police would have no authority to undertake an investigation. In the case of N Mahmud vs M Ahmed, 1984 BID (AD) 97 : 36 DLR (AD) 14, Badrul Haider Chowdhury, J referred to an earlier case Abdul Quader Chowdhury vs State 28 DLR (AD) 38 and took it to be a settled provision of law that there may be cases where allegation in the First Information Report or the complaint, even if they are taken at their face value and accepted in their entirety do not constitute the offence alleged and in such cases it would be legitimate for the High Court Division to hold that it would be manifestly unjust to allow process of the Criminal Court to be issued against an accused person. In that case Masud J observed that proceeding before a Court starts when the Magistrate takes cognisance of an offence on Police report or on complaint. Before such cognisance, there is no proceeding that may be quashed under section 561A  CrPC. Process is issued only after taking of cognizance. We are leaving this matter presently by pointing out that ordinarily the view taken by Masud J, is correct and the same is being followed in our Court since long. But that is not to say that the view expressed in 28 DLR (AD) 39, and referred to by Badrul Haider Chowdhury, J. is not correct. There may be one case out of a thousand where the High Court Division will be justified in interfering, even at the initial, stage before taking of cognizance. But the usual and well settled practice is that a criminal proceeding can only be quashed after cognisance has been taken and process issued thereupon subject to the fundamental principle that the power of quashing is and should be very sparingly exercised and only to prevent the abuse of the process of the Court." 

 84. In Abdul Huque and others vs State, 60 DLR (AD) 1, FIR was lodged by the then Bureau of Anti-Corruption under sections 409/420/109 of the Penal Code read with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 against the accused persons. Charge-sheet was submitted under the same sections of the law. The case was sent to the Court of Senior Metropolitan Special Judge, Dhaka where it was registered, but cognizance of the offence was not taken yet. Referring to the cases of Bangladesh vs Tan Kheng Hock, Nasiruddin Mahmud and Syed Mohammad Hashem alias Hashim the apex Court held,

It appears from the above discussion that except in the cases of Abdul Huque, 60 DLR (AD) 1 and Engineer Mosharrf Hossen, 21 BLC (AD) 211, it has been held in all other cases that if the FIR or the complaint does not disclose any offence, the High Court Division can exercise its extraordinary power under section 561A  to quash the FIR or the complaint even before taking cognizance of the offence by the competent Court. 

 92. Mr. Siddiqur Rahman Khan, on the other hand, points out that the observation made in Nasiruddin Mahmud, 36 DLR (AD) 14 by Chowdhury ATM Masud, J. was quoted and applied in Abdul Huque, 60 DLR (AD) 1. The learned Advocate further points out that in Syed Mohammad Hashem, 48 DLR (AD) 87 (which was also referred to and quoted in Abdul Huque), views expressed by Badrul Haider Chowdhury, J., who spoke for the majority in Nasiruddin Mahmud and that of Chowdhury ATM Masud, J. were held to be correct. Mr. Siddiqur Rahman submits that the principle laid down in Nasiruddin Mahmud and in Syed Mohammad Hashem that proceeding can be quashed at an early stage even before taking cognizance of the offence but in rarest of the rare cases is still a good law and the instant application for quashing the proceeding should be adjudicated on merit. The learned Advocate finally submits that the law declared in Abdul Huque and in Engineer Mosharrf Hossen, which are Anti-Corruption Commission cases, should be confined to facts and circumstances of those cases. 

 97. The offence of criminal breach of trust has been defined in section 405 of the Penal Code. The first ingredient Of the offence is entrustment with property or with dominion over property to the accused by the complainant. In Shamsul Alam and others vs AFR Hassan and others, 40 DLR 46, which was a case under sections 406 and 420 of the Penal, a question arose whether 'loan money' constituted 'entrustment' within the meaning of section 405. Arifur Rahman alias Bablu vs Shantosh Kumar Sadhu and another, 46 DLR (AD) 180, the accused requested the complainant to supply two trucks of jute at Taka 83,059 and assured him that he would pay Taka 40,000 in cash at the time of delivery and the rest Taka 43,059 within three days thereafter. The accused paid Taka 40,000. The complainant, in good faith, supplied the goods, but the accused did not pay the balance within three days. Later on, the accused refused to pay the balance money- It was held that inducement of part payment and specific promise to pay the balance within three days disclosed an offence.
